body.text: A US intelligence assessment should be setting off alarm bells in capitals across the Indo-Pacific. According to a 15 November report in The Wall Street Journal, the US intelligence community assesses that Iran retains 1,500 to 2,500 ballistic missiles, despite months of intensive US and Israeli military operations aimed, in part, at destroying those weapons.

The implications extend far beyond the Middle East. If the United States and Israel, with their overwhelming advantages in air power, intelligence and precision-strike capabilities, cannot eliminate the missile threat posed by Iran, how would the US and its allies fare against China, which possesses a substantially larger, more sophisticated and increasingly diverse missile arsenal?

This is not a theoretical question. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have demonstrated both the remarkable effectiveness of modern missile defences and their fundamental limitations. Systems such as Patriot, Thaad and Aegis have repeatedly intercepted sophisticated missile threats, saving lives and protecting critical military and civilian infrastructure.

But these successes have come at an enormous cost. The US and its allies are consuming expensive missile-defence interceptors far faster than their industries can replace them. And every interceptor expended in the Middle East is one that may not be available in a future Indo-Pacific conflict.
For Australia, Japan, South Korea and other US security partners, this growing mismatch between operational requirements and industrial capacity should be a major concern.

The strategic imperative is clear: the US and its partners must strengthen missile-defence capabilities, expand interceptor production and develop a more integrated allied defence industrial base before a major crisis occurs.
A warning from the Middle East

The central lesson from the conflict with Iran is that offensive military superiority does not guarantee the elimination of the threat of an adversary’s ground-based strike missiles, whether ballistic or cruise.

Despite extensive attacks against Iranian missile production facilities, launchers and supporting infrastructure, Tehran has demonstrated considerable resilience. Its surviving strike-missile inventory, dispersed infrastructure and ability to regenerate some production capacity show the difficulty of destroying a missile force through offensive operations alone.
The second lesson is equally important: successful missile defence requires large quantities of interceptors.

A recent analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates that about two-thirds of the US’s prewar Patriot interceptor stocks and around half of its Thaad interceptors have been expended in this year’s conflict with Iran. These are estimates rather than publicly confirmed Pentagon figures, but they illustrate the scale of the challenge.

The US is responding by seeking major increases in interceptor production. However, expanding manufacturing capacity, rebuilding specialised supply chains and training skilled workers will take years, not months.
Meanwhile, demand for these systems – including from Ukraine, the Middle East and US allies in the Indo-Pacific – continues to grow.
The unavoidable conclusion is that the US cannot assume it will have unlimited missile-defence resources available to support simultaneous crises in multiple theatres.
China’s missile challenge is substantially greater

The implications for the Indo-Pacific are particularly troubling. Iran has demonstrated that even an adversary whose technology is far inferior can preserve a substantial missile capability despite sustained offensive military operations, while forcing the US to expend large quantities of sophisticated defensive interceptors.

China, with its substantially larger missile forces, advanced military capabilities and extensive defence industry, could pose this challenge on an entirely different scale. Moreover, a conflict in the western Pacific would unfold across vast distances, further complicating the resupply of critical missile-defence systems.

According to the US Defense Intelligence Agency’s 2025 assessment, the People’s Liberation Army Rocket Force possessed about 900 short-range ballistic missiles, 1,300 medium-range ballistic missiles and 500 intermediate-range ballistic missiles, in addition to intercontinental ballistic missiles and ground-launched cruise missiles.

China’s military has also invested heavily in hypersonic weapons, sophisticated sensors, electromagnetic warfare and the ability to conduct coordinated strikes against US and allied military facilities.

In a potential conflict over Taiwan, Beijing could seek to overwhelm US and allied defences through large-scale, coordinated missile and drone attacks against air bases, ports, command-and-control facilities and other critical military infrastructure across the western Pacific.

The challenge would not simply involve intercepting individual missiles. It would involve sustaining defensive operations against repeated attacks while preserving sufficient interceptor inventories to protect critical assets throughout a prolonged conflict.

Moreover, unlike Iran, China could combine its missile attacks with sophisticated cyber operations, electronic warfare, counter-space capabilities and conventional military operations designed to degrade the sensors and command networks upon which missile defences depend.

As I argued in a previous article for The Strategist, the US has neglected important elements of its munitions industrial base for decades, creating critical shortages that now threaten the credibility of its deterrence commitments in the Indo-Pacific.

Indeed, while serving as a staff member on the US House Armed Services Committee nearly two decades ago, I reviewed a US military assessment indicating that the US needed about twice as many SM-3 and Thaad interceptors just to meet the minimum requirements identified by regional combatant commanders.
The problem was recognised then. Unfortunately, it was never adequately resolved.
The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have made these longstanding deficiencies substantially more urgent.
Five priorities for the US and its allies
First, the US must urgently replenish and expand its theatre missile-defence interceptor inventories.

Congress and the president should provide sustained funding and multi-year procurement contracts for Patriot, Thaad, SM-3 and other critical interceptors. The objective must be to create an industrial base capable not merely of meeting peacetime requirements but of sustaining prolonged, high-intensity combat.

Equally important, Washington should work with Indo-Pacific allies to establish realistic wartime stockpile requirements, including sufficient pre-positioned stocks to support operations during the opening phases of a conflict.
Second, the US must expand allied co-production of missile-defence interceptors.
This should be a central priority of Indo-Pacific defence industrial cooperation.

The US and Japan have already demonstrated the value of this approach through their successful joint development of the SM-3 Block IIA interceptor. In April 2026, the two countries reaffirmed plans to increase production of the interceptor by about four times and explore further expansion.
That cooperation should serve as a model for a broader regional effort.

Australia in particular should explore opportunities to participate in interceptor manufacturing, component production, maintenance and supply-chain development. Canberra’s Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance Enterprise, including its emerging domestic production of GMLRS munitions, provides an important foundation.
South Korea also has substantial advanced manufacturing capabilities and considerable experience developing indigenous air and missile-defence systems.

Expanding allied production would not only increase overall manufacturing capacity; it would also diversify supply chains, reduce dependence on a small number of US production facilities and improve the resilience of the allied defence industrial base during a crisis.

Such cooperation will require addressing technology-transfer restrictions, industrial security requirements and longstanding bureaucratic barriers. But these obstacles should not be allowed to prevent progress on a capability so central to regional deterrence.
Third, the US and its allies must accelerate investment in emerging missile-defence technologies.

The economics of missile defence are becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. Using interceptors costing millions of dollars to defeat inexpensive drones and other lower-cost threats creates an unfavourable cost-exchange ratio.

Directed-energy weapons, high-power microwaves, electronic warfare, autonomous interceptors and AI-enabled battle-management systems offer opportunities to reduce the cost of defending against certain classes of threats.

These capabilities will not replace high-performance kinetic interceptors needed to defeat sophisticated ballistic missiles. However, they can complement existing defences, particularly against drones and other lower-end threats, preserving scarce high-end interceptors for targets that genuinely require them.
Fourth, missile defence must be integrated into a broader missile defeat strategy.
The US and its allies cannot rely exclusively on intercepting missiles after they have been launched.

A credible strategy must also include capabilities to disrupt adversary missile operations before launch, including intelligence collection, cyber and electromagnetic warfare, and conventional strike options where appropriate and consistent with international law.

The goal should be to complicate an adversary’s ability to conduct large-scale missile attacks while reducing the burden on active missile-defence systems. This will require much closer integration of offensive and defensive planning among the US and its Indo-Pacific allies.
Fifth, allies must incorporate realistic interceptor expenditure and replenishment assumptions into military planning and exercises.
Too often, discussions of missile defence focus on the technical capabilities of individual systems rather than the operational challenges of sustaining them during prolonged combat.

Allied exercises should routinely assess how long current interceptor stocks could support defensive operations under different attack scenarios, how quickly replacement missiles could be delivered and how military commanders would prioritise the defence of critical assets when stocks become constrained.
These exercises should also test the resilience of regional logistics networks, command-and-control systems and industrial supply chains under wartime conditions.
Learn the lessons before the next crisis

As I have written elsewhere, the US and its allies should take considerable confidence from the operational performance of modern missile-defence systems in Ukraine and the Middle East. These systems have demonstrated that even sophisticated ballistic missile threats can be defeated.
But tactical success should not obscure the broader strategic challenge.
Missile-defence systems are only as effective as the sensors, command networks, trained personnel and interceptor inventories that sustain them.

China is undoubtedly studying the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, including the effectiveness of Western missile defences, their vulnerabilities and the rate at which the US and its allies are consuming critical munitions.

Beijing is also benefiting from expanding military and technological cooperation with Russia, Iran and North Korea, giving it additional opportunities to observe and absorb lessons from contemporary warfare.
If the US and Israel are having difficulty eliminating Iran’s missile threat, we should harbour no illusions about the much greater challenge posed by China.
The time to address the Indo-Pacific missile defence inventory problem is now – not after a conflict has begun and the magazines are running empty.
